scene-u01-pnew1-23.text: After this note you can do four things

scene-u01-pnew1-30.name: text#30
scene-u01-pnew1-30.text: say how a convolutional network differs from "flatten then fully connect"

scene-u01-pnew1-34.name: text#34
scene-u01-pnew1-34.text: say the three stages of a convolution layer and compute the output size and parameters

scene-u01-pnew1-38.name: text#38
scene-u01-pnew1-38.text: say what pooling does, what it costs and its three extensions

scene-u01-pnew1-42.name: text#42
scene-u01-pnew1-42.text: place the ten knowledge points of Week 6 on one map

scene-u01-pnew1-68.name: text#68
scene-u01-pnew1-68.text: Do these four things and you have learned KP00.

scene-u01-pnew2-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew2-26.text: Following the goals: first the main line.

scene-u01-pnew2-29.name: text#29
scene-u01-pnew2-29.text:
① Why not flatten?
neighbours and weight count

scene-u01-pnew2-31.name: text#31
scene-u01-pnew2-31.text:
② How is a conv layer computed?
output size and parameters

scene-u01-pnew2-33.name: text#33
scene-u01-pnew2-33.text:
③ What do pooling and the prior bring?
benefits and costs

scene-u01-pnew2-66.name: text#66
scene-u01-pnew2-66.text: All ten knowledge points answer these three questions.

scene-u01-pnew3-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew3-26.text: After the three questions: split the ten knowledge points into five stages.

scene-u01-pnew3-42.name: text#42
scene-u01-pnew3-42.text: KP01–KP02 → KP03–KP04, KP07 → KP05–KP06 → KP08–KP09 → KP10

scene-u01-pnew3-73.name: text#73
scene-u01-pnew3-73.text: Read along the arrows; every stage answers a small question.

scene-u01-pnew4-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew4-26.text: After the five stages: first the first question.

scene-u01-pnew4-31.name: text#31
scene-u01-pnew4-31.text: flattening loses neighbours and needs many weights; convolution connects neighbours and shares a kernel

scene-u01-pnew4-35.name: text#35
scene-u01-pnew4-35.text: LeNet: convolve and pool first, flatten last; $61{,}750$ parameters, $95.8\%$ fully connected (self-study)

scene-u01-pnew4-66.name: text#66
scene-u01-pnew4-66.text: Flattening throws neighbours away; LeNet shows a better skeleton.

scene-u01-pnew5-23.name: text#23
scene-u01-pnew5-23.text: Stage 2: how a convolution is computed (KP03, KP04, KP07)

scene-u01-pnew5-31.name: text#31
scene-u01-pnew5-31.text: three stages: convolution, detector, pooling; the kernel is learned by backprop

scene-u01-pnew5-35.name: text#35
scene-u01-pnew5-35.text: theory flips the kernel; code usually does not (cross-correlation), same power

scene-u01-pnew5-39.name: text#39
scene-u01-pnew5-39.text: output side $\lfloor\frac{d-f+2p}{s}\rfloor+1$; weights $f\times f\times C_{\mathrm{in}}\times C_{\mathrm{out}}$

scene-u01-pnew5-72.name: text#72
scene-u01-pnew5-72.text: A three-stage pipeline, cross-correlation without flipping, the output-side formula.

scene-u01-pnew6-23.name: text#23
scene-u01-pnew6-23.text: Stage 3: why so few parameters (KP05, KP06)

scene-u01-pnew6-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew6-26.text: After stage 2: it is cheap, so why?

scene-u01-pnew6-31.name: text#31
scene-u01-pnew6-31.text: sparse connectivity (mostly $0$) + parameter sharing (one set moved right)

scene-u01-pnew6-35.name: text#35
scene-u01-pnew6-35.text: shift then convolve = convolve then shift (equivariance, not invariance)

scene-u01-pnew6-37.name: text#37
scene-u01-pnew6-37.text: one shared kernel: fewer weights and equivariance

scene-u01-pnew6-66.name: text#66
scene-u01-pnew6-66.text: Most of the weight matrix is $0$ and the other rows are one set of weights moved to the right.

scene-u01-pnew7-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew7-26.text: After stage 3: the last two stations after convolution.

scene-u01-pnew7-31.name: text#31
scene-u01-pnew7-31.text: detector: activation per cell; pooling: one summary per window, no weights

scene-u01-pnew7-35.name: text#35
scene-u01-pnew7-35.text: approximate invariance + downsampling; harmful when position is the answer

scene-u01-pnew7-37.name: text#37
scene-u01-pnew7-37.text: convolution keeps position (equivariant), pooling blurs it (approx. invariant)

scene-u01-pnew7-70.name: text#70
scene-u01-pnew7-70.text: Pooling has no weights and buys approximate invariance and smaller feature maps.

scene-u01-pnew8-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew8-26.text: After stage 4: looking back, why does this design work?

scene-u01-pnew8-31.name: text#31
scene-u01-pnew8-31.text: infinitely strong prior: distant weights fixed to $0$ (a bet on sparsity)

scene-u01-pnew8-37.name: text#37
scene-u01-pnew8-37.text:
global average pooling
one number per map

scene-u01-pnew8-69.name: text#69
scene-u01-pnew8-69.text: Distant weights are fixed to $0$; GAP takes $25{,}088{,}000$ down to $512{,}000$.

scene-u01-pnew9-23.name: text#23
scene-u01-pnew9-23.text: One line through it all: the chapter in one sentence

scene-u01-pnew9-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew9-26.text: After the five stages: join the chapter into one sentence.

scene-u01-pnew9-34.name: text#34
scene-u01-pnew9-34.text:
pool to summarise
shrink the map

scene-u01-pnew9-40.name: text#40
scene-u01-pnew9-40.text: all of it is a "bet on sparsity" prior → the LeNet skeleton

scene-u01-pnew9-72.name: text#72
scene-u01-pnew9-72.text: Connect neighbours, share a kernel, detect per cell, summarise by pooling, then decide with fully connected layers.

scene-u01-pnew10-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew10-26.text: After the one-sentence summary: where to start reading?

first KP01
→ KP03 → KP04 → KP07
why and how

scene-u01-pnew10-31.text:
then KP05 → KP06
→ KP08 → KP09
fewer weights, pooling

scene-u01-pnew10-35.text: KP02 LeNet: self-study, readable at any time

scene-u01-pnew10-67.text: KP01 → KP03 → KP04 → KP07 → KP05 → KP06 → KP08 → KP09 → KP10.

scene-u01-pnew11-66.text: Week 7: how LeNet, AlexNet, VGG and ResNet stack the parts.

steps.label: KP00 · 1/11
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Four things first! There are four goals. The first and the second: say how a convolutional network differs from "flatten then fully connect"; say the three stages of a convolution layer and compute the output size and parameters.

steps.label: KP00 · 1/11 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Four things first! There are four goals. The first and the second: say how a convolutional network differs from "flatten then fully connect"; say the three stages of a convolution layer and compute the output size and parameters.

steps.label: KP00 · 1/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: The third: say what pooling does, what it costs and its three extensions.

steps.label: KP00 · 1/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: The fourth: place the ten knowledge points of Week 6 on one map. After reading, check yourself against these four.

steps.label: KP00 · 2/11
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Three questions! The first question: why should an image not be flattened and handed to a fully connected layer?

steps.label: KP00 · 2/11 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Three questions! The first question: why should an image not be flattened and handed to a fully connected layer?

steps.label: KP00 · 2/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: The second question: how is a convolution layer computed, how large is the output and how many parameters does it have?

steps.label: KP00 · 2/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: The third question: what do pooling and the prior bring and what do they cost? All ten knowledge points answer these three questions.

steps.label: KP00 · 3/11
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Five stages! The ten knowledge points fall into five stages: one, why convolve; two, how it is computed.

steps.label: KP00 · 3/11 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Five stages! The ten knowledge points fall into five stages: one, why convolve; two, how it is computed.

steps.label: KP00 · 3/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: Three, why there are so few parameters; four, what pooling does.

steps.label: KP00 · 3/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: Five, the infinitely strong prior and three extensions. Read along the arrows; every stage answers a small question.

steps.label: KP00 · 4/11
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Why convolve? KP01: after flattening a fully connected layer cannot tell which pixels are neighbours and must learn one weight per connection.

steps.label: KP00 · 4/11 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Why convolve? KP01: after flattening a fully connected layer cannot tell which pixels are neighbours and must learn one weight per connection.

steps.label: KP00 · 4/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: A convolution layer connects only neighbours and shares one kernel over the whole image, so it has far fewer weights and its feature map shifts when the input shifts.

steps.label: KP00 · 4/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: KP02: LeNet puts these parts together into a skeleton, with convolution and pooling in front and flattening only at the end, and sixty-one thousand seven hundred fifty parameters in total.

steps.label: KP00 · 5/11
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: How is it computed? KP03: a convolution layer has three stages, convolution, detector and pooling, and the numbers of the kernel are learned by backpropagation.

steps.label: KP00 · 5/11 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: How is it computed? KP03: a convolution layer has three stages, convolution, detector and pooling, and the numbers of the kernel are learned by backpropagation.

steps.label: KP00 · 5/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: KP04: theoretical convolution flips the kernel while code usually does not and computes cross-correlation; the two have the same expressive power.

steps.label: KP00 · 5/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: KP07: the output side is set by four knobs and the number of weights is f times f times input channels times output channels.

steps.label: KP00 · 6/11
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Why so few weights? KP05: a convolution layer is a fully connected layer whose weight matrix has two features: most of it is zero, which is sparse connectivity, and the other rows are one set of weights moved to the right, which is parameter sharing.

steps.label: KP00 · 6/11 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Why so few weights? KP05: a convolution layer is a fully connected layer whose weight matrix has two features: most of it is zero, which is sparse connectivity, and the other rows are one set of weights moved to the right, which is parameter sharing.

steps.label: KP00 · 6/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: KP06: because all positions share one kernel, shifting then convolving equals convolving then shifting, called translation equivariance.

steps.label: KP00 · 6/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: Equivariance holds for stride one, fails for rotation and scaling and is not translation invariance.

steps.label: KP00 · 7/11
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: What does pooling do? KP08: the detector applies an activation function once to every cell; pooling cuts the map into windows and keeps one summary per window with no learnable weights.

steps.label: KP00 · 7/11 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: What does pooling do? KP08: the detector applies an activation function once to every cell; pooling cuts the map into windows and keeps one summary per window with no learnable weights.

steps.label: KP00 · 7/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: KP09: when the input shifts right by one, the max-pooled output often has half unchanged, so it is approximately invariant to small local shifts; the feature map shrinks, reducing later cells and weights.

steps.label: KP00 · 7/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: The cost: when the position itself is the answer, the invariance of pooling does harm.

steps.label: KP00 · 8/11
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: The prior and extensions! KP10: convolution and pooling are an infinitely strong prior that structurally fixes the weights of distant connections to zero; this bet on sparsity lets the model generalise better.

steps.label: KP00 · 8/11 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: The prior and extensions! KP10: convolution and pooling are an infinitely strong prior that structurally fixes the weights of distant connections to zero; this bet on sparsity lets the model generalise better.

steps.label: KP00 · 8/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: Three extensions: dynamic pooling lets the pooling range follow the content; spatial pyramid pooling takes images of any size with a fixed number of bins; global average pooling squeezes every feature map into one number.

steps.label: KP00 · 8/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: For example with seven by seven by 512 into a thousand classes, global average pooling takes the weights from 25,088,000 down to 512,000, forty-nine times fewer.

steps.label: KP00 · 9/11
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: One line through it all! Join the chapter into one sentence: do not flatten the image, extract features with a convolution that connects only neighbours and shares one kernel.

steps.label: KP00 · 9/11 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: One line through it all! Join the chapter into one sentence: do not flatten the image, extract features with a convolution that connects only neighbours and shares one kernel.

steps.label: KP00 · 9/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: Then detect cell by cell and keep a summary by pooling to shrink the feature map.

steps.label: KP00 · 9/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: These restrictions are a prior that bets on sparsity, and only at the end is the map flattened and handed to fully connected layers to decide; LeNet is exactly this skeleton.

steps.label: KP00 · 10/11
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: A suggested reading order! A suggested order: read KP01 first to see why not to flatten; then KP03, KP04 and KP07 to learn how one convolution layer is computed.

steps.label: KP00 · 10/11 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: A suggested reading order! A suggested order: read KP01 first to see why not to flatten; then KP03, KP04 and KP07 to learn how one convolution layer is computed.

steps.label: KP00 · 10/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: Then KP05 and KP06 to see why it saves parameters and is equivariant; then KP08 and KP09 to learn pooling.

steps.label: KP00 · 10/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: Finally the prior and extensions of KP10. LeNet in KP02 is for self-study, puts the earlier parts back together and can be read at any time.

steps.label: KP00 · 11/11
steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Next week: classic architectures! All the parts of Week 6 are in place: convolution, the detector, pooling and the prior that bets on sparsity.

steps.speakerNotes: Think first: Next week: classic architectures! All the parts of Week 6 are in place: convolution, the detector, pooling and the prior that bets on sparsity.

steps.label: KP00 · 11/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Now the result: But how are these parts stacked into a complete network?

steps.label: KP00 · 11/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Finally: That is the topic of Week 7: classic architectures, LeNet, AlexNet, VGG and ResNet.
